\section{Introduction}

\subsection{The problem}

Let $\mathbb{F}_2^n$ denote the set of binary words of length $n$, equipped with the
\emph{Hamming distance} $d(x,y)=|\{j: x_j\neq y_j\}|$. A \emph{code} of length $n$ is a
subset $C\subseteq\mathbb{F}_2^n$; its \emph{minimum distance} is the least distance
between distinct codewords. A code of minimum distance $d$ detects any pattern of at
most $d-1$ errors and corrects any pattern of at most $\lfloor (d-1)/2\rfloor$ errors.
The fundamental extremal quantity is
\[
A(n,d)\;=\;\max\bigl\{\,|C| \;:\; C\subseteq \mathbb{F}_2^n,\ C \text{ has minimum distance} \ge d\,\bigr\}.
\]
Determining $A(n,d)$ exactly is open in general. This paper gives a complete,
self-contained development of the binary classical core of the theory, together with
three exact theorems---a rigidity classification, a perfection characterisation and a
collapse identity---that are the principal contributions.

\subsection{The word model and the length hypothesis}

We work with words as finite sequences of bits of unrestricted length, comparing two
words coordinatewise as far as both extend:
\[
d(x,y)\;=\;\#\{\, j<\min(|x|,|y|) \;:\; x_j\neq y_j\,\}.
\]
This makes $d$ total and symmetric, but the triangle inequality
$d(x,y)\le d(x,z)+d(z,y)$ can fail when the three words have different lengths, since a
short intermediate word truncates the comparison: with $x=00$, $y=11$ and $z$ the empty
word, $d(x,y)=2$ while $d(x,z)+d(z,y)=0$. Consequently \emph{every} metric statement
below carries an explicit equal-length hypothesis, and this is exactly the hypothesis
under which the truncation phenomenon disappears. Write
\[
W_n=\{\,x : |x|=n\,\},\qquad |W_n|=2^n .
\]
A code of length $n$ is a finite subset $C\subseteq W_n$. Without any hypothesis,
$d(x,y)=d(y,x)$ and $d(x,y)\le\min(|x|,|y|)$; if $|x|=|y|$ and $d(x,y)=0$ then $x=y$;
and if $|x|=|y|=|z|$ then $d(x,y)\le d(x,z)+d(z,y)$.

\begin{lemma}[Additivity over concatenation]\label{lem:append}
If $|x|=|y|$ then, for all words $p,q$,
$d(x\Vert p,\ y\Vert q)=d(x,y)+d(p,q)$, where $\Vert$ denotes concatenation.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
Induct on $x$. If $x$ and $y$ are empty both sides equal $d(p,q)$. The inductive step
peels one letter from each of $x,y$, contributing the same indicator to both sides.
\end{proof}

\section{Ball counting and sphere packing}

\begin{definition}
For $n,r\in\mathbb{N}$ and a word $c$, the \emph{Hamming ball} is
$B(n,r,c)=\{z\in W_n : d(z,c)\le r\}$.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[Ball Counting Lemma]\label{thm:ball}
For every $c$ with $|c|=n$,
\[
|B(n,r,c)| \;=\; V(n,r) \;:=\; \sum_{i=0}^{r}\binom{n}{i}.
\]
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Induct on $n$, peeling the leading letter. Write $c=b\Vert c'$ with $|c'|=n-1$. A word
$z\in W_n$ splits as $z=a\Vert z'$ with $d(z,c)=[a\neq b]+d(z',c')$, whence
\[
B(n,r,b\Vert c') \;=\; \bigl(b\Vert B(n-1,r,c')\bigr)\ \sqcup\ \bigl(\bar b\Vert B(n-1,r-1,c')\bigr),
\]
a disjoint union because the two parts differ in the leading letter. The base cases
$r=0$ and $n=0$ each give a single word. Taking cardinalities gives
$V(n,r)=V(n-1,r)+V(n-1,r-1)$, which is Pascal's rule for partial binomial sums.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[Homogeneity]\label{cor:homog}
If $|c|=|c'|=n$ then $|B(n,r,c)|=|B(n,r,c')|$.
\end{corollary}

\begin{definition}
A code $C$ has \emph{minimum distance at least $d$}, written $\MinDist(C,d)$, if
$d(x,y)\ge d$ for all distinct $x,y\in C$.
\end{definition}

\begin{proposition}[Packing]\label{prop:packing}
Let $C\subseteq W_n$ with $\MinDist(C,2t+1)$. Then the balls $B(n,t,x)$, $x\in C$, are
pairwise disjoint.
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
If $z\in B(n,t,x)\cap B(n,t,y)$ with $x\neq y$ then, all three words having length $n$,
$d(x,y)\le d(x,z)+d(z,y)\le 2t<2t+1$, a contradiction.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Sphere-packing / Hamming bound]\label{thm:sp}
If $C\subseteq W_n$ and $\MinDist(C,2t+1)$ then
$|C|\cdot\sum_{i=0}^{t}\binom{n}{i}\le 2^{n}$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
By Proposition~\ref{prop:packing} the union of the balls is disjoint, of cardinality
$|C|\cdot V(n,t)$ by Corollary~\ref{cor:homog}, and contained in $W_n$.
\end{proof}

\begin{definition}
A code $C\subseteq W_n$ with $\MinDist(C,2t+1)$ is \emph{perfect} (with radius $t$) if
$\bigcup_{x\in C}B(n,t,x)=W_n$, i.e.\ the balls tile.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[Equality case: packing implies tiling]\label{thm:tiling}
Let $C\subseteq W_n$ with $\MinDist(C,2t+1)$ and
$|C|\cdot\sum_{i=0}^{t}\binom{n}{i}=2^{n}$. Then $C$ is perfect.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
The union of the balls is contained in $W_n$ and, by disjointness, has cardinality
$|C|\cdot V(n,t)=2^n=|W_n|$; a subset of a finite set of equal cardinality is the whole
set.
\end{proof}

\section{The parity code and single-error detection}

\begin{definition}
The \emph{parity} of a word $l$ is $\pi(l)=l_0\oplus l_1\oplus\cdots$, the \textsc{xor}
of all its letters. The \emph{parity extension} is $\widehat{l}=l\Vert[\pi(l)]$.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[Parity is the mod-$2$ reduction of distance]\label{thm:parity}
If $|l|=|m|$ then $\pi(l)=\pi(m)$ if and only if $d(l,m)$ is even.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Induction on the common length: peeling leading letters $a,b$, the parity condition
flips exactly when $a\neq b$, and so does the parity of the distance.
\end{proof}

\begin{definition}
The \emph{parity code} of length $n+1$ is $P_n=\{\widehat{l} : l\in W_n\}$.
\end{definition}

Since $\widehat{\;\cdot\;}$ is injective, $|P_n|=2^n$, and $P_n\subseteq W_{n+1}$ with
$\pi(\widehat{l})=0$ for all $l$. By Lemma~\ref{lem:append},
$d(\widehat l,\widehat m)=d(l,m)+[\pi(l)\neq\pi(m)]$ whenever $|l|=|m|$.

\begin{theorem}[Minimum distance two]\label{thm:pmin}
$\MinDist(P_n,2)$, and for $n\ge 1$ the value $2$ is attained.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Distinct codewords have parity $0$, hence even distance by Theorem~\ref{thm:parity};
being nonzero it is at least $2$. For attainment take $l,m$ differing in one
coordinate: then $d(l,m)=1$, the parities differ, and $d(\widehat l,\widehat m)=2$.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Every single flip is detected]
If $|x|=|\widehat l|$ and $d(\widehat l,x)=1$ then $x\notin P_n$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
By Theorem~\ref{thm:parity}, $\pi(x)\neq\pi(\widehat l)=0$, while every element of $P_n$
has parity $0$.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[No single error is corrected]
For $n\ge 1$ there are $x\in W_{n+1}$ and distinct $c_1,c_2\in P_n$ with
$d(x,c_1)=d(x,c_2)=1$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Take $c_1,c_2$ at distance $2$ and let $x$ flip one of the two disagreeing coordinates
of $c_1$.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Optimality]\label{thm:detopt}
If $C\subseteq W_{n+1}$ and $\MinDist(C,2)$ then $|C|\le 2^n$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Two length-$(n+1)$ words agreeing away from the last coordinate are at distance at most
$1$; hence deletion of the last coordinate is injective on $C$ and embeds $C$ into
$W_n$.
\end{proof}

Thus $A(n+1,2)=2^n$, attained by $P_n$.

\section{The Hamming cube as a metric group}

\begin{definition}
For words $l,m$ let $l\oplus m$ be the coordinatewise \textsc{xor} (truncated to the
common length); $\wt(l)$ is the number of $1$'s in $l$, and $0_n$ is the zero word of
length $n$.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[Distance is the weight of the difference]\label{thm:wxor}
If $|l|=|m|$ then $d(l,m)=\wt(l\oplus m)$; in particular $d(l,0_n)=\wt(l)$ for $|l|=n$.
Moreover, for $|l|=|m|=n$ one has $l\oplus m=0_n$ if and only if $l=m$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Translation invariance]\label{thm:transl}
If $|x|=|y|=|z|=n$ then $d(x\oplus z,\ y\oplus z)=d(x,y)$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Induction on $n$: at each coordinate, $(a\oplus c)\neq (b\oplus c)$ iff $a\neq b$.
\end{proof}

Thus $(W_n,\oplus,d)$ is a metric group: an abelian group of exponent $2$ with a
translation-invariant metric, entirely determined by the weight function. Parity is a
homomorphism: $\pi(l\oplus m)=\pi(l)\oplus\pi(m)$ when $|l|=|m|$.

\begin{definition}
A code $C\subseteq W_n$ is \emph{linear} if $0_n\in C$ and $x\oplus y\in C$ for all
$x,y\in C$.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[Minimum distance equals minimum nonzero weight]\label{thm:linear}
Let $C\subseteq W_n$ be linear. Then
\[
\MinDist(C,d) \iff \bigl(\forall x\in C,\ x\neq 0_n \Rightarrow \wt(x)\ge d\bigr).
\]
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
($\Rightarrow$) For nonzero $x\in C$, $d\le d(x,0_n)=\wt(x)$ by
Theorem~\ref{thm:wxor}. ($\Leftarrow$) For distinct $x,y\in C$, closure gives
$x\oplus y\in C$, nonzero by Theorem~\ref{thm:wxor}, and translation invariance
(Theorem~\ref{thm:transl}) with $z=y$ gives $d(x,y)=\wt(x\oplus y)\ge d$.
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}
The hypothesis $0_n\in C$ is load-bearing in the backward direction: a coset
$a\oplus C$ has the same distance multiset but no zero word, and the weight condition
on it says nothing.
\end{remark}

\begin{theorem}[The parity code is the even-weight code]\label{thm:pareven}
$P_n=\{x\in W_{n+1} : \pi(x)=0\}$; it contains $0_{n+1}$ and is closed under $\oplus$.
Consequently every nonzero $x\in P_n$ has $\wt(x)\ge 2$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
The inclusion $\subseteq$ is $\pi(\widehat l)=0$. Conversely, if $\pi(x)=0$ and
$|x|=n+1$, write $x=l\Vert[b]$; then $b=\pi(l)$ and $x=\widehat l$. Linearity follows
from parity being a homomorphism, and the weight statement from
Theorem~\ref{thm:linear} with $d=2$ and Theorem~\ref{thm:pmin}.
\end{proof}

\section{Singleton and Gilbert--Varshamov}

\begin{lemma}[Prefix agreement bounds distance]\label{lem:prefix}
If $|x|=|y|=n$ and the length-$k$ prefixes of $x,y$ agree, then $d(x,y)\le n-k$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
Split $x=x_{<k}\Vert x_{\ge k}$ and likewise for $y$, and apply
Lemma~\ref{lem:append}: the first block contributes $0$ and the second at most $n-k$.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Singleton bound]\label{thm:singleton}
If $C\subseteq W_n$, $\MinDist(C,d)$ and $d\ge1$, then $|C|\le 2^{\,n+1-d}$, with
truncated subtraction (so the statement reads $|C|\le 1$ when $d>n+1$).
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Let $k=n+1-d$. Two distinct codewords with equal length-$k$ prefixes would satisfy
$d(x,y)\le n-k=d-1$ by Lemma~\ref{lem:prefix}, contradicting $\MinDist(C,d)$; in the
degenerate regime $d>n+1$ we have $k=0$, all prefixes agree, and the same argument
forces $|C|\le1$, which is what the right-hand side asserts. Hence prefix truncation is
injective from $C$ into the $2^k$ words of length $k$.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Gilbert--Varshamov bound]\label{thm:gv}
For all $n$ and all $d\ge1$ there exists $C\subseteq W_n$ with $\MinDist(C,d)$ and
$2^{n}\le |C|\cdot\sum_{i=0}^{d-1}\binom{n}{i}$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
The family of codes in $W_n$ with minimum distance $\ge d$ is finite and nonempty;
choose a member $C$ of maximum cardinality, hence maximal under inclusion. Every
$z\in W_n$ satisfies $d(z,x)\le d-1$ for some $x\in C$: otherwise $C\cup\{z\}$ would
again have minimum distance $\ge d$ and be strictly larger. So the radius-$(d-1)$ balls
cover $W_n$, and Theorem~\ref{thm:ball} gives $2^n\le|C|\cdot V(n,d-1)$.
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}
Theorem~\ref{thm:gv} is the exact converse of sphere packing: packing says radius-$t$
balls do not overlap, greed says radius-$(d-1)$ balls leave no gaps. Together they
bracket the extremal function,
\[
\frac{2^{n}}{V(n,d-1)} \;\le\; A(n,d) \;\le\; 2^{\,n+1-d}.
\]
The existence statement is not vacuous: the extracted code lies in $W_n$ and has
minimum distance $d$; for $d=1$ it returns all of $W_n$.
\end{remark}

\section{The Plotkin bound}

Sphere packing is vacuous when $2d>n$. That regime is covered by a double count.

\begin{lemma}[Coordinate form of the distance]\label{lem:coord}
If $|x|=|y|=n$ then $d(x,y)=\sum_{j=0}^{n-1}[\,x_j\neq y_j\,]$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{lemma}[One-coordinate pair count]\label{lem:paircount}
Let $C$ be a finite code and $c:C\to\{0,1\}$. If $k=|\{x\in C : c(x)=1\}|$ and $M=|C|$
then $\sum_{x\in C}\sum_{y\in C}[\,c(x)\neq c(y)\,]=2k(M-k)$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{theorem}[Upper estimate]\label{thm:tdu}
If $C\subseteq W_n$ then $2\sum_{x\in C}\sum_{y\in C}d(x,y)\le n\,|C|^{2}$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Exchange summation using Lemma~\ref{lem:coord} and apply Lemma~\ref{lem:paircount} at
each coordinate. The claim reduces to $4k(M-k)\le M^2$ for $0\le k\le M$, which upon
writing $M=k+f$ is $(k-f)^2\ge0$.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Lower estimate]\label{thm:tdl}
If $\MinDist(C,d)$ then $d\,|C|\,(|C|-1)\le\sum_{x\in C}\sum_{y\in C}d(x,y)$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
For fixed $x$ the inner sum has $|C|-1$ terms each at least $d$.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Plotkin bound]\label{thm:plotkin}
If $C\subseteq W_n$, $\MinDist(C,d)$ and $n<2d$, then $|C|(2d-n)\le 2d$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
With $M=|C|\ge1$, Theorems~\ref{thm:tdu} and~\ref{thm:tdl} give
$2dM(M-1)\le nM^{2}$; dividing by $M$ yields $2d(M-1)\le nM$, i.e.\ $M(2d-n)\le 2d$.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}
Under the hypotheses of Theorem~\ref{thm:plotkin}, $|C|\le 2d$, a bound independent of
the length. Moreover if $n<d$ then $|C|\le1$.
\end{corollary}

\begin{remark}
The hypothesis $n<2d$ is load-bearing: with truncated subtraction, dropping it
degenerates the conclusion into $0\le 2d$. Note also that the recursive view
$d(a\Vert x,b\Vert y)=[a\neq b]+d(x,y)$ powers the packing arguments while the
coordinate view of Lemma~\ref{lem:coord} powers the double counts; both are needed, and
it matters that they describe the same function.
\end{remark}

\section{Perfect single-error-correcting codes}

\subsection{The arithmetic obstruction}

\begin{theorem}[Necessity]\label{thm:necessity}
Let $C\subseteq W_n$ with $\MinDist(C,3)$ and suppose the radius-$1$ balls around the
codewords cover $W_n$. Then $n+1=2^{k}$ for some $k$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
The balls are disjoint (Proposition~\ref{prop:packing} with $t=1$) and cover, so
$|C|\cdot V(n,1)=2^{n}$ with $V(n,1)=n+1$. Hence $(n+1)\mid 2^{n}$, and since $2$ is
prime every divisor of $2^n$ is a power of two.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}
There is no perfect single-error-correcting binary code of length $4$: $5$ is not a
power of two.
\end{corollary}

\begin{corollary}
If $C\subseteq W_n$, $\MinDist(C,3)$ and $n+1$ is not a power of two, then
$|C|\cdot(n+1)<2^{n}$: sphere packing is strictly unattainable.
\end{corollary}

\subsection{The Hamming code without matrices}

Fix $k$ and set $n=2^k-1$. Index the coordinates by $1,2,\dots,2^k-1$: exactly the
nonzero $k$-bit patterns.

\begin{definition}[Syndrome]
For a word $z$ and a starting index $s$, set $\syn_s(\varepsilon)=0$ and
$\syn_s(a\Vert z')=(a\cdot s)\veebar \syn_{s+1}(z')$, where $\veebar$ is bitwise
\textsc{xor} of natural numbers and $a\cdot s$ is $s$ if $a=1$ and $0$ otherwise. Thus
$\syn_1(z)$ is the \textsc{xor} of the indices of the coordinates where $z$ has a $1$.
The \emph{Hamming code of order $k$} is
$\Ham_k=\{x\in W_{2^k-1} : \syn_1(x)=0\}$.
\end{definition}

\begin{lemma}[Homomorphism]\label{lem:synhom}
If $|x|=|y|$ then $\syn_s(x\oplus y)=\syn_s(x)\veebar\syn_s(y)$. Hence $\Ham_k$ is
linear.
\end{lemma}

\begin{lemma}[Low weights have nonzero syndrome]\label{lem:synlow}
If $1\le\wt(z)\le2$ and $s\ge1$ then $\syn_s(z)\neq0$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
A word of weight one has syndrome $s+i\ge1$ for the position $i$ of its $1$. A word of
weight two has syndrome $(s+i)\veebar(s+j)$ with $i\neq j$, and $a\veebar b=0$ iff
$a=b$.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Minimum distance three]\label{thm:hammin}
$\MinDist(\Ham_k,3)$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
$\Ham_k$ is linear and contains $0$, so by Theorem~\ref{thm:linear} it suffices that no
nonzero codeword has weight $1$ or $2$, which is Lemma~\ref{lem:synlow} with $s=1$.
\end{proof}

Lemma~\ref{lem:synlow} is precisely the classical requirement that the columns of the
parity-check matrix be distinct and nonzero; here it is a one-line property of
\textsc{xor}.

\begin{lemma}[Syndromes are legal positions]\label{lem:synlt}
If $s+|z|\le 2^{k}$ then $\syn_s(z)<2^{k}$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{theorem}[Covering and decoding]\label{thm:hamcover}
For every $x\in W_{2^k-1}$ there is $c\in\Ham_k$ with $d(x,c)\le1$: let
$v=\syn_1(x)$; if $v=0$ take $c=x$, otherwise flip coordinate $v$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
By Lemma~\ref{lem:synlt}, $v\le 2^k-1$, so the index exists. Flipping position $v$
changes the word by Hamming distance $1$ and the syndrome by $\veebar v$, yielding
$v\veebar v=0$.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Perfection, size, unique decoding]\label{thm:hamperf}
The radius-$1$ balls around the codewords of $\Ham_k$ tile $W_{2^k-1}$; consequently
$|\Ham_k|\cdot 2^{k}=2^{\,2^{k}-1}$, i.e.\ $|\Ham_k|=2^{\,2^k-1-k}$, and every received
word has exactly one codeword within distance $1$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Covering is Theorem~\ref{thm:hamcover}; disjointness is Proposition~\ref{prop:packing}
with Theorem~\ref{thm:hammin}; the size follows from $V(2^k-1,1)=2^k$ and
Theorem~\ref{thm:ball}. Uniqueness is disjointness.
\end{proof}

Note the size is an \emph{output} of the construction, forced by the tiling and the ball
count, rather than an input. For $k=2$, $\Ham_2=\{000,111\}$ is the triple repetition
code; for $k=3$ it is the $[7,4,3]$ code with $16$ codewords, sixteen balls of eight
words tiling the $128$-word cube.

\begin{theorem}[Existence characterisation]\label{thm:charac}
A perfect single-error-correcting binary code of length $n$ exists if and only if
$n+1=2^{k}$ for some $k$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Necessity is Theorem~\ref{thm:necessity}; sufficiency is
Theorem~\ref{thm:hamperf}.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Exact extremal values at Hamming lengths]\label{thm:Aham}
For every $k$, $A(2^k-1,3)=|\Ham_k|=2^{\,2^k-1-k}$; in particular $A(7,3)=16$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
The upper bound is sphere packing with $t=1$; the lower bound is $\Ham_k$.
\end{proof}

\section{Rigidity: the optimal detecting codes are exactly two}

\begin{definition}
The \emph{odd-weight code} is $O_n=\{x\in W_{n+1} : \pi(x)=1\}$.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}\label{thm:odd}
$|O_n|=2^n$, $\MinDist(O_n,2)$, and $O_n\neq P_n$ for every $n$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
The two parity classes partition $W_{n+1}$ and $|P_n|=2^n$, so $|O_n|=2^n$. Two
odd-parity words have equal parity, hence even distance, hence distance $\ge2$ if
distinct. Finally $0_{n+1}\in P_n\setminus O_n$.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Connectivity of the Hamming cube]\label{thm:conn}
Let $h:W_n\to\{0,1\}$ satisfy $h(x)=h(y)$ whenever $d(x,y)=1$. Then $h$ is constant.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Induct on $n$. For $n=0$ there is one word. For the step: $h$ restricted to words with
a fixed leading letter is constant by the inductive hypothesis applied to tails, since
prepending the same letter to two words at distance $1$ gives two words at distance
$1$; and $b\Vert z$ and $\bar b\Vert z$ are at distance $1$, so the two constants agree.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Parity is constant on an optimal detecting code]\label{thm:parconst}
Let $C\subseteq W_{n+1}$ with $\MinDist(C,2)$ and $|C|=2^n$. Then all codewords of $C$
have the same parity.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Deletion of the last coordinate, $x\mapsto x^{-}$, is injective on $C$ (proof of
Theorem~\ref{thm:detopt}) and lands in $W_n$; since $|C|=2^n=|W_n|$ it is a bijection
$C\to W_n$. Let $F:W_n\to C$ be its inverse, so $F(l)=l\Vert[p(l)]$ for a unique bit
$p(l)$.

Let $x,y\in W_n$ with $d(x,y)=1$. By Lemma~\ref{lem:append},
$d(F(x),F(y))=1+[\,p(x)\neq p(y)\,]$, and $F(x)\neq F(y)$, so minimum distance $2$
forces $p(x)\neq p(y)$. Also $\pi(x)\neq\pi(y)$, since $d(x,y)=1$ is odd
(Theorem~\ref{thm:parity}). Hence $\pi(F(x))=\pi(x)\oplus p(x)$ and
$\pi(F(y))=\pi(y)\oplus p(y)$ differ in both summands and are therefore equal. So
$l\mapsto\pi(F(l))$ is constant along edges, hence constant by Theorem~\ref{thm:conn};
as $F$ is onto $C$, all codewords share one parity.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Classification of optimal detecting codes]\label{thm:class}
Let $C\subseteq W_{n+1}$ with $\MinDist(C,2)$ and $|C|=2^n$. Then $C=P_n$ or $C=O_n$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
$C$ is nonempty; pick $c_0\in C$. By Theorem~\ref{thm:parconst} all codewords have
parity $\pi(c_0)$. If $\pi(c_0)=0$ then $C\subseteq P_n$ by Theorem~\ref{thm:pareven},
and $|C|=2^n=|P_n|$ forces equality; if $\pi(c_0)=1$ then similarly $C=O_n$.
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}
Both alternatives occur (Theorem~\ref{thm:odd}), and the cardinality hypothesis cannot
be dropped: any proper subset of $P_n$ has minimum distance $2$ but is neither $P_n$
nor $O_n$. The interpretation is a strong uniqueness statement about checksums: an
optimal single-error-detecting scheme must attach exactly the parity bit, up to a
single global complement.
\end{remark}

\section{The extremal function and the odd/even collapse}

\begin{definition}
$A(n,d)=\max\{|C| : C\subseteq W_n,\ \MinDist(C,d)\}$.
\end{definition}

The set of achievable sizes is nonempty (it contains $0$ via $C=\varnothing$) and
bounded by $2^n$, so $A(n,d)$ is a genuine maximum, attained by some code; and every
admissible code satisfies $|C|\le A(n,d)$.

\begin{theorem}[Extension raises odd distance]\label{thm:ext}
Let $C\subseteq W_n$ with $\MinDist(C,d)$ and $d$ odd. Then
$\widehat C=\{\widehat x : x\in C\}$ satisfies $\widehat C\subseteq W_{n+1}$,
$|\widehat C|=|C|$ and $\MinDist(\widehat C,d+1)$. Consequently
$A(n,d)\le A(n+1,d+1)$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Injectivity of the extension gives the cardinality. For distinct $x,y\in C$: if
$\pi(x)\neq\pi(y)$ then $d(\widehat x,\widehat y)=d(x,y)+1\ge d+1$; if $\pi(x)=\pi(y)$
then $d(\widehat x,\widehat y)=d(x,y)$, which is even by Theorem~\ref{thm:parity}, and
an even number at least the odd number $d$ is at least $d+1$.
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}
The naive argument ``$d\le d(x,y)$ so $d+1\le d(x,y)+1$'' is invalid, since the parity
bit need not always disagree. The evenness argument is the correct route, and it is
exactly where oddness enters.
\end{remark}

\begin{lemma}[Puncturing costs at most one]\label{lem:punct}
If $|x|=|y|$ then $d(x,y)\le d(x^{-},y^{-})+1$, where $x^{-}$ deletes the last
coordinate.
\end{lemma}

\begin{theorem}[Puncturing]\label{thm:punct}
Let $C\subseteq W_{n+1}$ with $\MinDist(C,d+1)$ and $d\ge1$. Then $x\mapsto x^{-}$ is
injective on $C$, its image lies in $W_n$ and has minimum distance $\ge d$.
Consequently $A(n+1,d+1)\le A(n,d)$, with no parity hypothesis.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
If $x^{-}=y^{-}$ with $x\neq y$ they differ only in the last coordinate, so
$d(x,y)\le1<d+1$. For the distance, $d+1\le d(x,y)\le d(x^{-},y^{-})+1$ by
Lemma~\ref{lem:punct}.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Odd/even collapse]\label{thm:collapse}
For every $n$ and every odd $d$, $A(n,d)=A(n+1,d+1)$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Combine Theorems~\ref{thm:ext} and~\ref{thm:punct}.
\end{proof}

Extension and puncturing are mutually inverse at the level of optimal codes; this is
the structural reason binary code tables list only odd minimum distances. Consequences:

\begin{itemize}
\item $A(n,1)=2^{n}$, since distance $1$ imposes no condition.
\item $A(n+1,2)=2^{n}$: a second, purely structural proof of the optimality of the
      parity code, from $A(n,1)=2^n$ and Theorem~\ref{thm:collapse} with $d=1$.
\item $A(8,4)=A(7,3)=16$: the extended Hamming code of length $8$ is optimal at
      distance $4$.
\item $A(2^{k},4)=A(2^k-1,3)=2^{\,2^k-1-k}$: all extended Hamming codes are optimal.
\item $A(n,e)\le A(n,d)$ for $d\le e$, and $A(n+j,d+j)\le A(n,d)$ for all $j$ and all
      $d\ge1$ (iterated puncturing, a Singleton-type decay).
\end{itemize}

\begin{theorem}[The oddness hypothesis is necessary]
$A(4,3)<A(3,2)$; hence Theorem~\ref{thm:collapse} fails for $d=2$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
$A(3,2)=4$; and sphere packing with $t=1$, $n=4$ gives $|C|\cdot5\le16$, so
$A(4,3)\le3$.
\end{proof}

In words: no minimum-distance-$2$ code of length $3$ and size $4$ extends to a
minimum-distance-$3$ code of length $4$. Puncturing always works; extension needs
oddness. Odd distances are the primitive ones, which is why sphere packing is naturally
stated at $d=2t+1$.

\section{Algorithms and applications}

\paragraph{Syndrome decoding.} Given a received word $x$ of length $2^k-1$: compute
$v=\syn_1(x)$, the \textsc{xor} of the indices $i$ with $x_i=1$; if $v=0$ accept $x$,
otherwise flip coordinate $v$ and accept. Cost: $O(n)$ \textsc{xor} operations, $O(1)$
memory, no tables. Correctness is Theorem~\ref{thm:hamcover}, and
Theorem~\ref{thm:hamperf} guarantees the answer is the unique codeword within distance
$1$. This is the algorithm behind single-error-correcting ECC memory; the extended
Hamming code of length $2^k$ (Theorem~\ref{thm:ext}) yields the familiar
correct-one/detect-two behaviour, and Theorem~\ref{thm:collapse} explains why that
extension is free.

\paragraph{Greedy construction.} The proof of Theorem~\ref{thm:gv} is an algorithm:
scan the $2^n$ words in any order, adding a word whenever it is at distance $\ge d$
from all previously chosen words. The result is maximal, hence of size at least
$2^n/V(n,d-1)$; the cost is $O(2^n\,|C|\,n)$.

\paragraph{Bound comparison.} The three upper bounds
\[
U_{\mathrm{SP}}=\Bigl\lfloor \tfrac{2^n}{V(n,\lfloor (d-1)/2\rfloor)}\Bigr\rfloor,\quad
U_{\mathrm{Sing}}=2^{\,n+1-d},\quad
U_{\mathrm{Plot}}=\Bigl\lfloor \tfrac{2d}{2d-n}\Bigr\rfloor\ (n<2d)
\]
have complementary regimes: sphere packing is strongest for small $d$ relative to $n$,
Singleton in the intermediate range, and Plotkin as $d$ approaches and exceeds $n/2$.
Their minimum, together with the Gilbert--Varshamov lower bound, produces the classical
bracketing table for $A(n,d)$, exact at $(n,1)$, $(n+1,2)$, $(2^k-1,3)$, $(2^k,4)$ and
in particular at $(7,3)$ and $(8,4)$.

\section{Discussion and open problems}

A single recursion---peel the leading coordinate---produces both the ball count
(Theorem~\ref{thm:ball}) and the connectivity of the cube (Theorem~\ref{thm:conn}).
Ball counting produces sphere packing above and, via greedy maximality,
Gilbert--Varshamov below. Splitting a word into blocks (Lemma~\ref{lem:append})
produces Singleton, puncturing and extension. Double counting produces Plotkin. The
equality case of packing converts a numerical identity into a tiling; the tiling
converts into a divisibility; and the divisibility, with the primality of $2$,
eliminates infinitely many lengths at a stroke, while the syndrome construction shows
the remaining lengths all occur.

\paragraph{Conjecture 1 (Equality in Plotkin and Hadamard matrices).} Equality in
$|C|(2d-n)\le2d$ at $n=2d-1$ forces every coordinate to split the code exactly in half
(the estimate $4k(M-k)\le M^2$ must be tight at every coordinate, i.e.\ $M=2k$) and
every pair of codewords to be at distance exactly $d$; written as $\pm1$ vectors the
codewords are then pairwise orthogonal, i.e.\ a Hadamard matrix. We conjecture that
$A(2d-1,d)=2d$ holds exactly when a Hadamard matrix of order $2d$ exists. First
instances: $A(3,2)=4$ (parity code) and $A(7,4)=8$ (punctured Hadamard code) hold,
while no length-$5$, distance-$3$ code of size $6$ exists. The double-count proof
already isolates the two inequalities whose equality cases are needed.

\paragraph{Conjecture 2 (Binary MDS codes are trivial).} A code attaining
$|C|=2^{\,n+1-d}$ with $2\le d\le n$ should be either the whole even-weight code
($d=2$) or the repetition code ($d=n$). The puncturing map of
Theorem~\ref{thm:singleton} is a bijection in the equality case, so every shortening of
an MDS code is again MDS; iterating reduces any putative example to a length-$d$ code
of size $2$, and the parity/repetition dichotomy is the base case.

\paragraph{Conjecture 3 (Uniqueness of the Hamming code).} For $k\ge2$, any
$C\subseteq W_{2^k-1}$ with minimum distance $3$ and $|C|=2^{\,2^k-1-k}$ should equal
$\Ham_k$ up to a permutation of coordinates. Perfection is forced by
Theorem~\ref{thm:tiling}, so the content is that the tiling determines the code up to
symmetry.

Beyond these: the Elias--Bassalygo and linear-programming bounds, which need a
genuinely different, harmonic-analytic technique; the classification of all perfect
binary codes, where the Golay code $[23,12,7]$ enters; nonbinary alphabets, where
$V(n,r)=\sum_i\binom{n}{i}(q-1)^i$ and the same architecture goes through; and
asymptotics, where the Gilbert--Varshamov and sphere-packing bounds become the
classical entropy-rate inequalities.

Binary codes: bounds, rigidity and perfection.
=============================================

A self-contained numerical demonstration of the results developed in the
accompanying paper.  Every function is inlined; the only dependency is the
Python standard library.

The objects.  A *word* is a tuple of bits.  The *Hamming distance* between two
words of the same length is the number of positions where they disagree.  A
*code* of length n is a set of words of length n; its *minimum distance* is the
smallest distance between two distinct codewords.

The results demonstrated here.

  1. Ball counting lemma:   |B(n,r,c)| = sum_{i<=r} C(n,i), independent of c.
  2. Sphere-packing bound:  |C| * V(n,t) <= 2^n  when mindist >= 2t+1.
  3. Singleton bound:       |C| <= 2^(n+1-d).
  4. Gilbert-Varshamov:     a greedy code satisfies |C| * V(n,d-1) >= 2^n.
  5. Plotkin bound:         |C| * (2d-n) <= 2d  when n < 2d.
  6. Parity code:           |P_n| = 2^n, minimum distance exactly 2, optimal.
  7. Rigidity:              the only length-(n+1) distance-2 codes of size 2^n
                            are the even-weight and the odd-weight codes.
  8. Linear criterion:      minimum distance = minimum nonzero weight.
  9. Hamming codes:         syndrome = XOR of the indices of the ones;
                            minimum distance 3, perfect, |H_k| = 2^(2^k-1-k).
 10. Perfection:            a perfect 1-error-correcting binary code of length
                            n exists iff n+1 is a power of two.
 11. Odd/even collapse:     A(n,d) = A(n+1,d+1) for odd d; and A(4,3) < A(3,2)
                            shows the oddness hypothesis cannot be dropped.
"""

from __future__ import annotations

from itertools import combinations, product
from math import comb
from typing import List, Optional, Sequence, Set, Tuple

Word = Tuple[int, ...]
Code = List[Word]


# --------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 1.  The metric
# --------------------------------------------------------------------------

def hdist(x: Word, y: Word) -> int:
    """Hamming distance, comparing coordinatewise over the common prefix.

    For equal-length words this is the usual Hamming metric.  (For unequal
    lengths the comparison truncates, and the triangle inequality can fail --
    which is why every statement below is applied to equal-length words only.)
    """
    return sum(1 for a, b in zip(x, y) if a != b)


def weight(x: Word) -> int:
    """Hamming weight: the number of ones."""
    return sum(x)


def xor_word(x: Word, y: Word) -> Word:
    """Coordinatewise XOR: the group operation of the Hamming cube."""
    return tuple(a ^ b for a, b in zip(x, y))


def parity(x: Word) -> int:
    """The XOR of all letters: 1 iff the weight is odd."""
    return weight(x) % 2


def words(n: int) -> List[Word]:
    """All 2^n binary words of length n."""
    return [tuple(w) for w in product((0, 1), repeat=n)]


def min_distance(code: Sequence[Word]) -> Optional[int]:
    """Minimum distance of a code (None if it has fewer than two words)."""
    if len(code) < 2:
        return None
    return min(hdist(x, y) for x, y in combinations(code, 2))


# --------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 2.  Balls and the counting lemma
# --------------------------------------------------------------------------

def ball(n: int, r: int, c: Word) -> List[Word]:
    """All length-n words within Hamming distance r of c."""
    return [z for z in words(n) if hdist(z, c) <= r]


def ball_volume(n: int, r: int) -> int:
    """V(n,r) = sum_{i=0}^{r} C(n,i)."""
    return sum(comb(n, i) for i in range(min(r, n) + 1))


def demo_ball_counting(max_n: int = 8) -> None:
    print("=" * 74)
    print("1.  BALL COUNTING LEMMA   |B(n,r,c)| = sum_{i<=r} C(n,i)")
    print("=" * 74)
    print("    Verified for every centre c, so the cube is homogeneous.\n")
    print(f"    {'n':>3} {'r':>3} {'formula':>10} {'all centres agree':>20}")
    for n in range(0, max_n + 1):
        for r in range(0, n + 1):
            sizes = {len(ball(n, r, c)) for c in words(n)}
            formula = ball_volume(n, r)
            assert sizes == {formula}, (n, r, sizes, formula)
        print(f"    {n:>3} {n:>3} {ball_volume(n, n):>10} {'yes':>20}")
    print("\n    Pascal recursion V(n+1,r) = V(n,r) + V(n,r-1):")
    for n in range(1, 6):
        for r in range(1, n + 1):
            assert ball_volume(n, r) == ball_volume(n - 1, r) + ball_volume(n - 1, r - 1)
    print("    verified for all 1 <= r <= n <= 5.\n")


# --------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 3.  The four bounds
# --------------------------------------------------------------------------

def sphere_packing_bound(n: int, d: int) -> int:
    """Largest |C| allowed by sphere packing:  floor(2^n / V(n,t)), t=(d-1)//2."""
    t = (d - 1) // 2
    return (2 ** n) // ball_volume(n, t)


def singleton_bound(n: int, d: int) -> int:
    """2^(n+1-d), with truncated subtraction (so it reads 1 when d > n+1)."""
    return 2 ** max(0, n + 1 - d)


def plotkin_bound(n: int, d: int) -> Optional[int]:
    """floor(2d / (2d - n)) when n < 2d; None otherwise (bound not applicable)."""
    if n >= 2 * d:
        return None
    return (2 * d) // (2 * d - n)


def gilbert_varshamov_lower(n: int, d: int) -> int:
    """Ceiling of 2^n / V(n,d-1): the guaranteed size of a greedy code."""
    v = ball_volume(n, d - 1)
    return -((-(2 ** n)) // v)


def greedy_code(n: int, d: int) -> Code:
    """Greedy (Gilbert-Varshamov) construction: scan all words, keep any word
    at distance >= d from everything already chosen.  The result is maximal,
    hence its radius-(d-1) balls cover the cube."""
    chosen: Code = []
    for z in words(n):
        if all(hdist(z, c) >= d for c in chosen):
            chosen.append(z)
    return chosen


def brute_force_A(n: int, d: int) -> int:
    """Exact A(n,d) by exhaustive search over maximal cliques.  Feasible only
    for very small n; used here to confirm A(3,2)=4 and A(4,3)=2."""
    universe = words(n)
    best = 0

    def extend(current: Code, start: int) -> None:
        nonlocal best
        best = max(best, len(current))
        remaining = len(universe) - start
        if len(current) + remaining <= best:
            return
        for i in range(start, len(universe)):
            z = universe[i]
            if all(hdist(z, c) >= d for c in current):
                current.append(z)
                extend(current, i + 1)
                current.pop()

    extend([], 0)
    return best


def demo_bounds(max_n: int = 8) -> None:
    print("=" * 74)
    print("2-5.  THE FOUR BOUNDS ON A(n,d)")
    print("=" * 74)
    print("    SP = sphere packing, Sing = Singleton, Plot = Plotkin (n<2d),")
    print("    GV = Gilbert-Varshamov lower bound, greedy = size actually built.\n")
    header = f"    {'n':>3} {'d':>3} {'GV':>6} {'greedy':>7} | {'SP':>7} {'Sing':>7} {'Plot':>7} {'best UB':>8}"
    print(header)
    print("    " + "-" * (len(header) - 4))
    for n in range(3, max_n + 1):
        for d in range(2, n + 1):
            g = greedy_code(n, d)
            assert (min_distance(g) or d) >= d
            sp = sphere_packing_bound(n, d)
            sing = singleton_bound(n, d)
            plot = plotkin_bound(n, d)
            ubs = [sp, sing] + ([plot] if plot is not None else [])
            best_ub = min(ubs)
            gv = gilbert_varshamov_lower(n, d)
            assert len(g) >= gv, (n, d, len(g), gv)
            assert len(g) <= best_ub, (n, d, len(g), best_ub)
            ps = "-" if plot is None else str(plot)
            print(f"    {n:>3} {d:>3} {gv:>6} {len(g):>7} | {sp:>7} {sing:>7} {ps:>7} {best_ub:>8}")
        print()
    print("    Note the regimes: sphere packing wins for small d, Singleton in")
    print("    the middle, Plotkin once d approaches n/2.\n")


# --------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 4.  The parity code, the odd-weight code, and rigidity
# --------------------------------------------------------------------------

def with_parity(l: Word) -> Word:
    """Append the parity bit."""
    return l + (parity(l),)


def parity_code(n: int) -> Code:
    """The even-weight code of length n+1: all parity extensions of W_n."""
    return [with_parity(l) for l in words(n)]


def odd_code(n: int) -> Code:
    """The odd-weight code of length n+1."""
    return [x for x in words(n + 1) if parity(x) == 1]


def all_optimal_detecting_codes(n: int) -> List[Set[Word]]:
    """Exhaustively list every length-(n+1) code with minimum distance 2 and
    exactly 2^n codewords.  The rigidity theorem predicts exactly two."""
    universe = words(n + 1)
    target = 2 ** n
    found: List[Set[Word]] = []

    def extend(current: Code, start: int) -> None:
        if len(current) == target:
            found.append(set(current))
            return
        if len(current) + (len(universe) - start) < target:
            return
        for i in range(start, len(universe)):
            z = universe[i]
            if all(hdist(z, c) >= 2 for c in current):
                current.append(z)
                extend(current, i + 1)
                current.pop()

    extend([], 0)
    return found


def demo_parity_and_rigidity(n: int = 3) -> None:
    print("=" * 74)
    print("6-7.  THE PARITY CODE, AND RIGIDITY OF THE OPTIMUM")
    print("=" * 74)
    for m in range(1, 6):
        P = parity_code(m)
        O = odd_code(m)
        print(f"    n+1 = {m+1:>2}:  |P| = {len(P):>3} = 2^{m},  mindist(P) = {min_distance(P)},"
              f"   |O| = {len(O):>3},  mindist(O) = {min_distance(O)}")
        assert len(P) == 2 ** m and min_distance(P) == 2
        assert len(O) == 2 ** m and min_distance(O) == 2
    print()
    print(f"    Exhaustive search over all length-{n+1} codes of minimum distance 2")
    print(f"    with exactly 2^{n} = {2**n} codewords:")
    optima = all_optimal_detecting_codes(n)
    P, O = set(parity_code(n)), set(odd_code(n))
    print(f"      number of optimal codes found : {len(optima)}")
    print(f"      equals {{even-weight, odd-weight}} : {sorted(map(sorted, optima)) == sorted(map(sorted, [P, O]))}")
    assert len(optima) == 2 and {frozenset(P), frozenset(O)} == {frozenset(c) for c in optima}
    print("    -> exactly the two codes predicted by the classification theorem.\n")
    print("    A single flip is always detected, never corrected:")
    c = with_parity((1, 0, 1))
    x = (c[0] ^ 1,) + c[1:]
    print(f"      codeword {c}, received {x}: parity {parity(x)} (nonzero) -> flagged")
    nbrs = [w for w in parity_code(3) if hdist(w, x) == 1]
    print(f"      but {len(nbrs)} codewords sit at distance 1 from it -> cannot correct\n")


# --------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 5.  Linear codes: distance = minimum nonzero weight
# --------------------------------------------------------------------------

def is_linear(code: Sequence[Word], n: int) -> bool:
    """Contains the zero word and is closed under coordinatewise XOR."""
    S = set(code)
    if tuple([0] * n) not in S:
        return False
    return all(xor_word(x, y) in S for x in S for y in S)


def min_nonzero_weight(code: Sequence[Word]) -> Optional[int]:
    ws = [weight(x) for x in code if weight(x) > 0]
    return min(ws) if ws else None


def demo_linear_criterion() -> None:
    print("=" * 74)
    print("8.  LINEAR CODES: MINIMUM DISTANCE = MINIMUM NONZERO WEIGHT")
    print("=" * 74)
    print("    Comparing |C| choose 2 distances against |C|-1 weights.\n")
    print(f"    {'code':>22} {'linear':>7} {'mindist':>8} {'minwt':>6} {'pairs':>7} {'weights':>8}")
    samples = [("parity code, n+1=5", parity_code(4), 5),
               ("Hamming H_2 (rep. 3)", hamming_code(2), 3),
               ("Hamming H_3 = [7,4,3]", hamming_code(3), 7),
               ("Hamming H_4 = [15,11,3]", hamming_code(4), 15)]
    for name, C, n in samples:
        lin = is_linear(C, n)
        md, mw = min_distance(C), min_nonzero_weight(C)
        assert lin and md == mw
        print(f"    {name:>22} {str(lin):>7} {md:>8} {mw:>6}"
              f" {len(C)*(len(C)-1)//2:>7} {len(C)-1:>8}")
    print("\n    A coset shows why the zero word is needed: shift H_3 by a fixed word.")
    shift = (1, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0)
    coset = [xor_word(shift, c) for c in hamming_code(3)]
    print(f"      coset minimum distance    : {min_distance(coset)}  (unchanged)")
    print(f"      coset minimum weight      : {min_nonzero_weight(coset)}  (now meaningless)\n")


# --------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 6.  Hamming codes via syndrome = XOR of indices
# --------------------------------------------------------------------------

def syndrome(x: Word) -> int:
    """XOR of the 1-based indices of the coordinates carrying a one."""
    s = 0
    for i, bit in enumerate(x, start=1):
        if bit:
            s ^= i
    return s


def hamming_code(k: int) -> Code:
    """All words of length 2^k - 1 with vanishing syndrome."""
    n = 2 ** k - 1
    return [x for x in words(n) if syndrome(x) == 0]


def hamming_decode(x: Word) -> Word:
    """Syndrome decoding: compute v = XOR of the indices of the ones; if v = 0
    accept, else flip coordinate v (1-based).  O(n) time, O(1) memory."""
    v = syndrome(x)
    if v == 0:
        return x
    y = list(x)
    y[v - 1] ^= 1
    return tuple(y)


def demo_hamming(max_k: int = 4) -> None:
    print("=" * 74)
    print("9.  HAMMING CODES: SYNDROME = XOR OF THE INDICES OF THE ONES")
    print("=" * 74)
    print(f"    {'k':>2} {'n=2^k-1':>8} {'|H_k|':>7} {'2^(n-k)':>9} {'mindist':>8}"
          f" {'|H|*V(n,1)':>11} {'2^n':>8} {'perfect':>8}")
    for k in range(1, max_k + 1):
        n = 2 ** k - 1
        H = hamming_code(k)
        md = min_distance(H)
        vol = ball_volume(n, 1)
        covered = {z for c in H for z in ball(n, 1, c)} if n <= 15 else None
        perfect = (len(H) * vol == 2 ** n)
        if covered is not None and n <= 7:
            assert len(covered) == 2 ** n
        assert len(H) == 2 ** (n - k)
        assert md is None or md >= 3
        print(f"    {k:>2} {n:>8} {len(H):>7} {2**(n-k):>9} {str(md):>8}"
              f" {len(H)*vol:>11} {2**n:>8} {str(perfect):>8}")
    print("\n    Decoding every single-bit corruption of every [7,4,3] codeword:")
    H = hamming_code(3)
    total = 0
    for c in H:
        for i in range(7):
            r = list(c)
            r[i] ^= 1
            assert hamming_decode(tuple(r)) == c
            total += 1
    print(f"      {total} corrupted words, all decoded back to the sent codeword.")
    print("    Two-bit corruptions are, of course, mis-decoded (distance 3 only")
    print("    guarantees correction of one error):")
    c = H[5]
    r = list(c)
    r[0] ^= 1
    r[3] ^= 1
    print(f"      sent {c}, received {tuple(r)}, decoded {hamming_decode(tuple(r))}\n")
    print("    H_2 is exactly the triple repetition code:")
    print(f"      H_2 = {sorted(hamming_code(2))}\n")


# --------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 7.  Which lengths admit a perfect code?
# --------------------------------------------------------------------------

def is_power_of_two(m: int) -> bool:
    return m > 0 and (m & (m - 1)) == 0


def demo_perfection(max_n: int = 16) -> None:
    print("=" * 74)
    print("10.  PERFECT 1-ERROR-CORRECTING CODES EXIST IFF n+1 IS A POWER OF TWO")
    print("=" * 74)
    print("    A perfect code needs |C|*(n+1) = 2^n, so (n+1) must divide 2^n,")
    print("    and a divisor of a power of two is a power of two.\n")
    print(f"    {'n':>3} {'n+1':>4} {'(n+1) | 2^n':>12} {'n+1 = 2^k':>10} {'perfect code exists':>21}")
    for n in range(1, max_n + 1):
        div = (2 ** n) % (n + 1) == 0
        pw = is_power_of_two(n + 1)
        assert div == pw
        print(f"    {n:>3} {n+1:>4} {str(div):>12} {str(pw):>10} {str(pw):>21}")
    print("\n    Length 4 in detail: balls of radius 1 hold 5 words, and 5 does not")
    print("    divide 16, so no tiling of the 4-cube by such balls can exist.")
    print(f"      sphere-packing bound A(4,3) <= {sphere_packing_bound(4,3)},"
          f"  exhaustive maximum = {brute_force_A(4,3)}")
    print(f"      strict inequality |C|*(n+1) < 2^n :"
          f" {brute_force_A(4,3)*5} < 16 -> {brute_force_A(4,3)*5 < 16}\n")


# --------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 8.  The extremal function and the odd/even collapse
# --------------------------------------------------------------------------

def demo_collapse() -> None:
    print("=" * 74)
    print("11.  ODD/EVEN COLLAPSE:  A(n,d) = A(n+1,d+1) FOR ODD d")
    print("=" * 74)
    print("    Extension (append a parity bit) raises an odd distance by one;")
    print("    puncturing (delete the last bit) lowers any distance by at most one.\n")
    print("    Exact values from the theory:")
    rows = [("A(n,1)", "2^n", "distance 1 is no condition"),
            ("A(n+1,2)", "2^n", "parity code, and it is optimal"),
            ("A(7,3)", "16", "the [7,4,3] Hamming code"),
            ("A(8,4)", "16", "extension of the above; collapse with d=3"),
            ("A(2^k-1,3)", "2^(2^k-1-k)", "Hamming code of order k"),
            ("A(2^k,4)", "2^(2^k-1-k)", "extended Hamming code")]
    for a, b, why in rows:
        print(f"      {a:>12} = {b:<14}  ({why})")
    print()
    print("    Extension in action: take the [7,4,3] code and append parity bits.")
    H = hamming_code(3)
    E = [with_parity(c) for c in H]
    print(f"      |H_3| = {len(H)}, mindist = {min_distance(H)}")
    print(f"      |extended| = {len(E)}, length {len(E[0])}, mindist = {min_distance(E)}")
    assert len(E) == len(H) and min_distance(E) == 4
    print("      all distances in the extended code are even, so 3 is forced up to 4.")
    print()
    print("    Puncturing in action: delete the last bit of the extended code.")
    Pc = [c[:-1] for c in E]
    print(f"      |punctured| = {len(set(Pc))}, length {len(Pc[0])}, mindist = {min_distance(Pc)}")
    assert set(Pc) == set(H)
    print("      we get exactly H_3 back: the two maps are mutually inverse here.")
    print()
    print("    The oddness hypothesis cannot be dropped:")
    a32, a43 = brute_force_A(3, 2), brute_force_A(4, 3)
    print(f"      A(3,2) = {a32}  (even distance d = 2)")
    print(f"      A(4,3) = {a43}  <  {a32}   -> A(n,d) = A(n+1,d+1) FAILS for even d")
    assert a43 < a32
    print()

# 9.  Total-distance double count behind the Plotkin bound
# --------------------------------------------------------------------------

def total_pairwise_distance(code: Sequence[Word]) -> int:
    """S = sum over ordered pairs of d(x,y)."""
    return sum(hdist(x, y) for x in code for y in code)


def demo_plotkin_double_count() -> None:

from __future__ import annotations

from itertools import combinations, product
from math import comb
from typing import List, Optional, Sequence, Set, Tuple

Word = Tuple[int, ...]
Code = List[Word]


# --------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 1.  The metric
# --------------------------------------------------------------------------

def hdist(x: Word, y: Word) -> int:
    """Hamming distance, comparing coordinatewise over the common prefix.

    For equal-length words this is the usual Hamming metric.  (For unequal
    lengths the comparison truncates, and the triangle inequality can fail --
    which is why every statement below is applied to equal-length words only.)
    """
    return sum(1 for a, b in zip(x, y) if a != b)


def weight(x: Word) -> int:
    """Hamming weight: the number of ones."""
    return sum(x)


def xor_word(x: Word, y: Word) -> Word:
    """Coordinatewise XOR: the group operation of the Hamming cube."""
    return tuple(a ^ b for a, b in zip(x, y))


def parity(x: Word) -> int:
    """The XOR of all letters: 1 iff the weight is odd."""
    return weight(x) % 2


def words(n: int) -> List[Word]:
    """All 2^n binary words of length n."""
    return [tuple(w) for w in product((0, 1), repeat=n)]


def min_distance(code: Sequence[Word]) -> Optional[int]:
    """Minimum distance of a code (None if it has fewer than two words)."""
    if len(code) < 2:
        return None
    return min(hdist(x, y) for x, y in combinations(code, 2))


# --------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 2.  Balls and the counting lemma
# --------------------------------------------------------------------------

def ball(n: int, r: int, c: Word) -> List[Word]:
    """All length-n words within Hamming distance r of c."""
    return [z for z in words(n) if hdist(z, c) <= r]


def ball_volume(n: int, r: int) -> int:
    """V(n,r) = sum_{i=0}^{r} C(n,i)."""
    return sum(comb(n, i) for i in range(min(r, n) + 1))


def demo_ball_counting(max_n: int = 8) -> None:
    print("=" * 74)
    print("1.  BALL COUNTING LEMMA   |B(n,r,c)| = sum_{i<=r} C(n,i)")
    print("=" * 74)
    print("    Verified for every centre c, so the cube is homogeneous.\n")
    print(f"    {'n':>3} {'r':>3} {'formula':>10} {'all centres agree':>20}")
    for n in range(0, max_n + 1):
        for r in range(0, n + 1):
            sizes = {len(ball(n, r, c)) for c in words(n)}
            formula = ball_volume(n, r)
            assert sizes == {formula}, (n, r, sizes, formula)
        print(f"    {n:>3} {n:>3} {ball_volume(n, n):>10} {'yes':>20}")
    print("\n    Pascal recursion V(n+1,r) = V(n,r) + V(n,r-1):")
    for n in range(1, 6):
        for r in range(1, n + 1):
            assert ball_volume(n, r) == ball_volume(n - 1, r) + ball_volume(n - 1, r - 1)
    print("    verified for all 1 <= r <= n <= 5.\n")


# --------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 3.  The four bounds
# --------------------------------------------------------------------------

def sphere_packing_bound(n: int, d: int) -> int:
    """Largest |C| allowed by sphere packing:  floor(2^n / V(n,t)), t=(d-1)//2."""
    t = (d - 1) // 2
    return (2 ** n) // ball_volume(n, t)


def singleton_bound(n: int, d: int) -> int:
    """2^(n+1-d), with truncated subtraction (so it reads 1 when d > n+1)."""
    return 2 ** max(0, n + 1 - d)


def plotkin_bound(n: int, d: int) -> Optional[int]:
    """floor(2d / (2d - n)) when n < 2d; None otherwise (bound not applicable)."""
    if n >= 2 * d:
        return None
    return (2 * d) // (2 * d - n)


def gilbert_varshamov_lower(n: int, d: int) -> int:
    """Ceiling of 2^n / V(n,d-1): the guaranteed size of a greedy code."""
    v = ball_volume(n, d - 1)
    return -((-(2 ** n)) // v)


def greedy_code(n: int, d: int) -> Code:
    """Greedy (Gilbert-Varshamov) construction: scan all words, keep any word
    at distance >= d from everything already chosen.  The result is maximal,
    hence its radius-(d-1) balls cover the cube."""
    chosen: Code = []
    for z in words(n):
        if all(hdist(z, c) >= d for c in chosen):
            chosen.append(z)
    return chosen


def brute_force_A(n: int, d: int) -> int:
    """Exact A(n,d) by exhaustive search over maximal cliques.  Feasible only
    for very small n; used here to confirm A(3,2)=4 and A(4,3)=2."""
    universe = words(n)
    best = 0

    def extend(current: Code, start: int) -> None:
        nonlocal best
        best = max(best, len(current))
        remaining = len(universe) - start
        if len(current) + remaining <= best:
            return
        for i in range(start, len(universe)):
            z = universe[i]
            if all(hdist(z, c) >= d for c in current):
                current.append(z)
                extend(current, i + 1)
                current.pop()

    extend([], 0)
    return best


def demo_bounds(max_n: int = 8) -> None:
    print("=" * 74)
    print("2-5.  THE FOUR BOUNDS ON A(n,d)")
    print("=" * 74)
    print("    SP = sphere packing, Sing = Singleton, Plot = Plotkin (n<2d),")
    print("    GV = Gilbert-Varshamov lower bound, greedy = size actually built.\n")
    header = f"    {'n':>3} {'d':>3} {'GV':>6} {'greedy':>7} | {'SP':>7} {'Sing':>7} {'Plot':>7} {'best UB':>8}"
    print(header)
    print("    " + "-" * (len(header) - 4))
    for n in range(3, max_n + 1):
        for d in range(2, n + 1):
            g = greedy_code(n, d)
            assert (min_distance(g) or d) >= d
            sp = sphere_packing_bound(n, d)
            sing = singleton_bound(n, d)
            plot = plotkin_bound(n, d)
            ubs = [sp, sing] + ([plot] if plot is not None else [])
            best_ub = min(ubs)
            gv = gilbert_varshamov_lower(n, d)
            assert len(g) >= gv, (n, d, len(g), gv)
            assert len(g) <= best_ub, (n, d, len(g), best_ub)
            ps = "-" if plot is None else str(plot)
            print(f"    {n:>3} {d:>3} {gv:>6} {len(g):>7} | {sp:>7} {sing:>7} {ps:>7} {best_ub:>8}")
        print()
    print("    Note the regimes: sphere packing wins for small d, Singleton in")
    print("    the middle, Plotkin once d approaches n/2.\n")


# --------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 4.  The parity code, the odd-weight code, and rigidity
# --------------------------------------------------------------------------

def with_parity(l: Word) -> Word:
    """Append the parity bit."""
    return l + (parity(l),)


def parity_code(n: int) -> Code:
    """The even-weight code of length n+1: all parity extensions of W_n."""
    return [with_parity(l) for l in words(n)]


def odd_code(n: int) -> Code:
    """The odd-weight code of length n+1."""
    return [x for x in words(n + 1) if parity(x) == 1]


def all_optimal_detecting_codes(n: int) -> List[Set[Word]]:
    """Exhaustively list every length-(n+1) code with minimum distance 2 and
    exactly 2^n codewords.  The rigidity theorem predicts exactly two."""
    universe = words(n + 1)
    target = 2 ** n
    found: List[Set[Word]] = []

    def extend(current: Code, start: int) -> None:
        if len(current) == target:
            found.append(set(current))
            return
        if len(current) + (len(universe) - start) < target:
            return
        for i in range(start, len(universe)):
            z = universe[i]
            if all(hdist(z, c) >= 2 for c in current):
                current.append(z)
                extend(current, i + 1)
                current.pop()

    extend([], 0)
    return found


def demo_parity_and_rigidity(n: int = 3) -> None:
    print("=" * 74)
    print("6-7.  THE PARITY CODE, AND RIGIDITY OF THE OPTIMUM")
    print("=" * 74)
    for m in range(1, 6):
        P = parity_code(m)
        O = odd_code(m)
        print(f"    n+1 = {m+1:>2}:  |P| = {len(P):>3} = 2^{m},  mindist(P) = {min_distance(P)},"
              f"   |O| = {len(O):>3},  mindist(O) = {min_distance(O)}")
        assert len(P) == 2 ** m and min_distance(P) == 2
        assert len(O) == 2 ** m and min_distance(O) == 2
    print()
    print(f"    Exhaustive search over all length-{n+1} codes of minimum distance 2")
    print(f"    with exactly 2^{n} = {2**n} codewords:")
    optima = all_optimal_detecting_codes(n)
    P, O = set(parity_code(n)), set(odd_code(n))
    print(f"      number of optimal codes found : {len(optima)}")
    print(f"      equals {{even-weight, odd-weight}} : {sorted(map(sorted, optima)) == sorted(map(sorted, [P, O]))}")

# 5.  Linear codes: distance = minimum nonzero weight
# --------------------------------------------------------------------------

def is_linear(code: Sequence[Word], n: int) -> bool:
    """Contains the zero word and is closed under coordinatewise XOR."""
    S = set(code)
    if tuple([0] * n) not in S:
        return False
    return all(xor_word(x, y) in S for x in S for y in S)


def min_nonzero_weight(code: Sequence[Word]) -> Optional[int]:
    ws = [weight(x) for x in code if weight(x) > 0]
    return min(ws) if ws else None

# --------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 6.  Hamming codes via syndrome = XOR of indices
# --------------------------------------------------------------------------

def syndrome(x: Word) -> int:
    """XOR of the 1-based indices of the coordinates carrying a one."""
    s = 0
    for i, bit in enumerate(x, start=1):
        if bit:
            s ^= i
    return s


def hamming_code(k: int) -> Code:
    """All words of length 2^k - 1 with vanishing syndrome."""
    n = 2 ** k - 1
    return [x for x in words(n) if syndrome(x) == 0]


def hamming_decode(x: Word) -> Word:
    """Syndrome decoding: compute v = XOR of the indices of the ones; if v = 0
    accept, else flip coordinate v (1-based).  O(n) time, O(1) memory."""
    v = syndrome(x)
    if v == 0:
        return x
    y = list(x)
    y[v - 1] ^= 1
    return tuple(y)

def is_power_of_two(m: int) -> bool:
    return m > 0 and (m & (m - 1)) == 0

def total_pairwise_distance(code: Sequence[Word]) -> int:

from __future__ import annotations

from math import comb
from typing import Dict, List, Optional, Tuple


# ----------------------------------------------------------------------
# bounds
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------

def ball_volume(n: int, r: int) -> int:
    return sum(comb(n, i) for i in range(max(0, min(r, n)) + 1))


def sphere_packing_bound(n: int, d: int) -> int:
    return (2 ** n) // ball_volume(n, (d - 1) // 2)


def singleton_bound(n: int, d: int) -> int:
    return 2 ** max(0, n + 1 - d)


def plotkin_bound(n: int, d: int) -> Optional[int]:
    return None if n >= 2 * d else (2 * d) // (2 * d - n)


def gilbert_varshamov_lower(n: int, d: int) -> int:
    return -((-(2 ** n)) // ball_volume(n, d - 1))


def composite_upper(n: int, d: int) -> Tuple[int, str]:
    cands: List[Tuple[int, str]] = [(sphere_packing_bound(n, d), "sphere packing"),
                                    (singleton_bound(n, d), "Singleton")]
    p = plotkin_bound(n, d)
    if p is not None:
        cands.append((p, "Plotkin"))
    if n < d:
        cands.append((1, "trivial"))
    return min(cands, key=lambda z: z[0])


# ----------------------------------------------------------------------
# exact search
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------

def popcount(x: int) -> int:
    return bin(x).count("1")


def exact_A(n: int, d: int) -> Tuple[int, List[int]]:
    """Exact A(n,d) and an optimal code, words held as integer bitmasks.

    This is a maximum-clique computation on the graph whose vertices are the
    words of length n at distance >= d from the all-zero word, with an edge
    whenever two words are at distance >= d.  Translation invariance of the
    Hamming metric lets us assume the all-zero word is a codeword, which cuts
    the search space by a factor of 2^n.

    The search is a Tomita-style branch and bound: vertex sets are Python
    integers used as bitsets, and the branching order is produced by a greedy
    colouring that also supplies the pruning bound (a clique cannot be larger
    than the number of colour classes available).
    """
    if d <= 1:
        return 2 ** n, list(range(2 ** n))
    if d > n:
        return 1, [0]

    verts = [z for z in range(1, 2 ** n) if popcount(z) >= d]
    m = len(verts)
    adj = [0] * m
    for a in range(m):
        for b in range(a + 1, m):
            if popcount(verts[a] ^ verts[b]) >= d:
                adj[a] |= 1 << b
                adj[b] |= 1 << a

    best_size = 0
    best_clique: List[int] = []

    def colour_sort(mask: int) -> List[Tuple[int, int]]:
        """Greedy colouring: return (vertex, colour) in nondecreasing colour."""
        order: List[Tuple[int, int]] = []
        colour = 0
        remaining = mask
        while remaining:
            colour += 1
            avail = remaining
            while avail:
                low = avail & -avail
                v = low.bit_length() - 1
                avail &= ~low
                avail &= ~adj[v]
                remaining &= ~low
                order.append((v, colour))
        return order

    def expand(mask: int, clique: List[int]) -> None:
        nonlocal best_size, best_clique
        if not mask:
            if len(clique) > best_size:
                best_size, best_clique = len(clique), clique[:]
            return
        for v, colour in reversed(colour_sort(mask)):
            if len(clique) + colour <= best_size:
                return
            clique.append(v)
            expand(mask & adj[v], clique)
            clique.pop()
            mask &= ~(1 << v)

    expand((1 << m) - 1, [])
    return best_size + 1, [0] + [verts[i] for i in best_clique]

# report
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------

def main(max_n: int = 8) -> None:
    print("=" * 78)
    print("EXACT VALUES OF A(n,d) BY EXHAUSTIVE SEARCH, AGAINST THE BOUNDS")
    print("=" * 78)
    print(f"{'n':>3} {'d':>3} {'GV':>6} {'A(n,d)':>8} {'upper':>7} {'winner':>15} {'corridor closed':>16}")

    print("  A(n+1,2) = 2^n for every computed n:              confirmed")
    for n in range(2, max_n + 1):

from typing import List, Tuple

Word = Tuple[int, ...]


def syndrome(x: Word) -> int:
    """XOR of the 1-based indices of the coordinates carrying a one."""
    s = 0
    for i, bit in enumerate(x, start=1):

            s ^= i

def is_codeword(x: Word) -> bool:
    """A word belongs to the Hamming code exactly when its syndrome vanishes."""
    return syndrome(x) == 0


def parity_positions(k: int) -> List[int]:
    """The check positions are the powers of two: 1, 2, 4, ..., 2^(k-1)."""
    return [1 << j for j in range(k)]


def hamming_encode(message: Word, k: int) -> Word:
    """Place the message bits in the non-power-of-two positions of a length
    (2^k - 1) word, then set each check bit so that the syndrome vanishes.

    The check position 2^j is the unique coordinate whose index contributes bit
    j and nothing else, so the check bits can be solved for one at a time.
    """
    n = 2 ** k - 1
    checks = set(parity_positions(k))
    data_positions = [i for i in range(1, n + 1) if i not in checks]
    if len(message) != len(data_positions):
        raise ValueError(f"message must have {len(data_positions)} bits")
    word = [0] * n
    for bit, pos in zip(message, data_positions):
        word[pos - 1] = bit
    s = syndrome(tuple(word))
    for j in range(k):
        if (s >> j) & 1:
            word[(1 << j) - 1] ^= 1
    assert syndrome(tuple(word)) == 0
    return tuple(word)


def hamming_decode(received: Word) -> Tuple[Word, int]:
    """Return (corrected word, index of the flipped coordinate, 0 if none).

    Compute v = syndrome(received).  If v = 0 the word is already a codeword.
    Otherwise coordinate v (1-based) is the unique single flip that returns the
    word to the code, and it is applied.
    """
    v = syndrome(received)
    if v == 0:
        return received, 0
    corrected = list(received)
    corrected[v - 1] ^= 1
    return tuple(corrected), v


def hamming_extract(codeword: Word, k: int) -> Word:
    """Read the message bits back out of a codeword."""
    checks = set(parity_positions(k))
    return tuple(b for i, b in enumerate(codeword, start=1) if i not in checks)


def _self_test(k: int = 4) -> None:
    """Every single-bit corruption of every codeword decodes back correctly."""
    from itertools import product

    n = 2 ** k - 1
    data_len = n - k
    for message in product((0, 1), repeat=min(data_len, 8)):
        msg = message + (0,) * (data_len - len(message))
        c = hamming_encode(msg, k)
        assert hamming_decode(c) == (c, 0)
        for i in range(n):
            r = list(c)
            r[i] ^= 1
            fixed, pos = hamming_decode(tuple(r))
            assert fixed == c and pos == i + 1
        assert hamming_extract(c, k) == msg
    print(f"self-test passed for k = {k} (length {n}, {data_len} message bits)")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    _self_test(3)
    _self_test(4)

from math import comb
from typing import List, Tuple

Word = Tuple[int, ...]


def ball_volume(n: int, r: int) -> int:

    return sum(comb(n, i) for i in range(min(r, n) + 1))

    """Greedy maximal code, words represented as integers in [0, 2^n)."""

def ball_volume(n: int, r: int) -> int:

    t = (d - 1) // 2

def singleton_bound(n: int, d: int) -> int:
    return 2 ** max(0, n + 1 - d)

    if n >= 2 * d:

    return (2 * d) // (2 * d - n)

        (singleton_bound(n, d), "Singleton"),

    if p is not None:
        candidates.append((p, "Plotkin"))
    t = trivial_bound(n, d)
    if t is not None:
        candidates.append((t, "trivial"))
    return min(candidates, key=lambda pair: pair[0])

      <p>
        Number the coordinates <code>1, 2, …, 2<sup>k</sup>−1</code>: these are exactly
        the nonzero <em>k</em>-bit patterns. Write <code>s(x)</code> for the XOR of the
        indices where <code>x</code> has a one. Two facts do everything.
      </p>
      <p>
        <strong>XOR is additive.</strong> <code>s(x ⊕ y) = s(x) ⊕ s(y)</code>. So if a
        codeword <code>c</code> (with <code>s(c)=0</code>) is corrupted by an error
        pattern <code>e</code>, the received word <code>r = c ⊕ e</code> has
        <code>s(r) = s(e)</code>: the syndrome sees the error and nothing else.
      </p>
      <p>
        <strong>Distinct nonzero indices never cancel.</strong> <code>a ⊕ b = 0</code>
        only when <code>a = b</code>. So a single error at position <code>i</code> gives
        <code>s(r) = i</code> — the syndrome literally <em>is</em> the address of the
        broken bit. And an error pattern of weight 1 or 2 always has nonzero syndrome,
        which is why the minimum distance of the code is at least 3.
      </p>
      <p>

        <code>e = e<sub>i</sub> ⊕ e<sub>j</sub></code> the syndrome is
        <code>i ⊕ j</code>, a perfectly legal single address — so the decoder confidently
        flips a third, innocent, bit. Distance 3 buys exactly one correction, no more.

"use strict";

/* ---------- core arithmetic: syndrome = XOR of indices of the ones ---------- */

function syndrome(bits) {
  let s = 0;
  for (let i = 0; i < bits.length; i++) if (bits[i]) s ^= (i + 1);
  return s;
}
function weight(bits) { return bits.reduce((a, b) => a + b, 0); }
function isCheckPos(i1) { return (i1 & (i1 - 1)) === 0; }   // 1-based index a power of two
function hdist(a, b) { let d = 0; for (let i = 0; i < a.length; i++) if (a[i] !== b[i]) d++; return d; }

function randomCodeword(k) {
  const n = (1 << k) - 1;
  const w = new Array(n).fill(0);
  for (let i = 1; i <= n; i++) if (!isCheckPos(i)) w[i - 1] = Math.random() < 0.5 ? 1 : 0;
  let s = syndrome(w);
  for (let j = 0; j < k; j++) if ((s >> j) & 1) w[(1 << j) - 1] ^= 1;
  return w;
}

function decode(bits) {
  const v = syndrome(bits);
  if (v === 0) return { word: bits.slice(), pos: 0 };
  const y = bits.slice();
  y[v - 1] ^= 1;
  return { word: y, pos: v };
}

/* ---------- state ---------- */

let k = 3;
let sent = randomCodeword(k);
let cur = sent.slice();

const $ = id => document.getElementById(id);

/* ---------- the bit strip ---------- */

function renderBits() {
  const host = $("bits");
  host.innerHTML = "";
  const dec = decode(cur);
  cur.forEach((b, idx) => {
    const i1 = idx + 1;
    const el = document.createElement("div");
    el.className = "bit" + (b ? " one" : "") + (isCheckPos(i1) ? " check" : "");
    if (cur[idx] !== sent[idx]) el.classList.add("flipped");
    if (dec.pos === i1) el.classList.add("fix");
    el.innerHTML = `<div class="v">${b}</div><div class="i">${i1}</div>`;
    el.title = (isCheckPos(i1) ? "check position " : "message position ") + i1;
    el.onclick = () => { cur[idx] ^= 1; renderAll(); };
    host.appendChild(el);
  });
}

function renderVerdict() {
  const v = syndrome(cur);
  const dec = decode(cur);
  const d = hdist(cur, sent);
  $("synval").textContent = v;
  $("synbin").textContent = v.toString(2).padStart(k, "0");
  $("wt").textContent = weight(cur);
  $("dist").textContent = d;
  const box = $("verdict");
  if (v === 0 && d === 0) {
    box.className = "verdict ok";
    box.innerHTML = "<strong>Syndrome 0.</strong> This is a codeword — nothing to repair.";
  } else if (v === 0 && d > 0) {
    box.className = "verdict err";
    box.innerHTML = "<strong>Syndrome 0, but " + d + " bits were flipped.</strong> " +
      "You have landed on a <em>different</em> codeword: the error pattern was itself a codeword, " +
      "so it is completely invisible. This needs at least " + d + " flips, and the minimum distance is 3.";
  } else {
    const correct = dec.word.every((b, i) => b === sent[i]);
    box.className = correct ? "verdict ok" : "verdict warn";
    box.innerHTML = "<strong>Syndrome " + v + " = " + v.toString(2).padStart(k, "0") +
      "<sub>2</sub>.</strong> The decoder flips coordinate " + v + " — highlighted in green. " +
      (correct
        ? "That restores the word you started from. One error, correctly repaired."
        : "But you flipped " + d + " bits, and the decoder is only entitled to assume one. " +
          "It repairs to the <em>nearest</em> codeword, which is not the one you sent: " +
          "this is the miscorrection that distance 3 permits.");
  }
}

/* ---------- the tiling picture ---------- */

const PALETTE = ["#1f4e79","#a83232","#2e7d32","#b8860b","#6a4c93","#118ab2","#e07a5f","#3d5a80",
                 "#8e6c88","#43aa8b","#d1495b","#577590","#9c6644","#7f5539","#4f772d","#bc4749",
                 "#255c99","#c1666b","#48a9a6","#e4b363","#8ac926","#ff924c","#5f0f40","#9a031e",
                 "#0f4c5c","#5c4d7d","#b56576","#355070","#6d597a","#e56b6f","#eaac8b","#264653"];

function renderCube() {
  const n = (1 << k) - 1;
  const host = $("cube");
  host.innerHTML = "";
  if (n > 7) {
    host.style.display = "none";
    $("cubelegend").textContent =
      "The picture is drawn for lengths up to 7; at length " + n + " the cube has " +
      Math.pow(2, n) + " words, tiled by " + Math.pow(2, n - k) + " balls of " + (n + 1) + " words each.";
    $("cubesize").textContent = Math.pow(2, n);
    $("cubelen").textContent = n;
    $("tileEq").textContent = "|C| · " + (n + 1) + " = " + Math.pow(2, n);
    return;
  }
  host.style.display = "grid";
  host.style.gridTemplateColumns = "repeat(" + (n === 3 ? 4 : 16) + ", 1fr)";
  const total = 1 << n;
  const centres = [];
  for (let m = 0; m < total; m++) {
    const bits = [];
    for (let i = n - 1; i >= 0; i--) bits.push((m >> i) & 1);
    const c = decode(bits).word;
    let ci = 0;
    for (let i = 0; i < n; i++) ci = (ci << 1) | c[i];
    if (!centres.includes(ci)) centres.push(ci);
    const cell = document.createElement("div");
    cell.className = "cell" + (syndrome(bits) === 0 ? " centre" : "");
    cell.style.background = PALETTE[centres.indexOf(ci) % PALETTE.length];
    cell.title = bits.join("") + "  →  " + c.join("");
    host.appendChild(cell);
  }
  $("cubesize").textContent = total;
  $("cubelen").textContent = n;
  $("tileEq").textContent = "|C| · " + (n + 1) + " = " + total;
  $("cubelegend").textContent =
    centres.length + " colour classes × " + (n + 1) + " words each = " +
    (centres.length * (n + 1)) + " = " + total + " words. Exactly a tiling.";
}

/* ---------- the statistics table ---------- */

function renderStats() {
  const n = (1 << k) - 1;
  const size = Math.pow(2, n - k);
  const rows = [
    ["length <em>n</em>", n + " = 2<sup>" + k + "</sup> − 1"],
    ["number of codewords", size + " = 2<sup>" + (n - k) + "</sup>"],
    ["message bits / check bits", (n - k) + " / " + k],
    ["minimum distance", "3 — corrects one error, detects two"],
    ["ball volume V(n,1)", (n + 1) + " = 2<sup>" + k + "</sup>"],
    ["tiling identity", size + " × " + (n + 1) + " = " + Math.pow(2, n) + " = 2<sup>" + n + "</sup>"],
    ["extremal value A(" + n + ",3)", size + " — no larger code of this length and distance exists"],
    ["extended code", "append a parity bit: length " + (n + 1) + ", distance 4, same " + size +
      " codewords (A(" + (n + 1) + ",4) = A(" + n + ",3))"]
  ];
  $("stats").innerHTML = "<tr><th>quantity</th><th>value</th></tr>" +
    rows.map(r => "<tr><td>" + r[0] + "</td><td class='mono'>" + r[1] + "</td></tr>").join("");
}

function renderAll() { renderBits(); renderVerdict(); }

/* ---------- controls ---------- */

$("korder").onchange = e => {
  k = parseInt(e.target.value, 10);
  sent = randomCodeword(k); cur = sent.slice();
  renderAll(); renderCube(); renderStats();
};
$("randmsg").onclick = () => { sent = randomCodeword(k); cur = sent.slice(); renderAll(); };
$("reset").onclick = () => { cur = sent.slice(); renderAll(); };
$("rand1").onclick = () => {
  cur = sent.slice();
  cur[Math.floor(Math.random() * cur.length)] ^= 1;
  renderAll();
};
$("rand2").onclick = () => {
  cur = sent.slice();
  const n = cur.length;
  let i = Math.floor(Math.random() * n), j = Math.floor(Math.random() * n);
  while (j === i) j = Math.floor(Math.random() * n);
  cur[i] ^= 1; cur[j] ^= 1;
  renderAll();
};

renderAll(); renderCube(); renderStats();
</script>
</body>
</html>

        <input type="range" id="n" min="2" max="24" value="7">
        <div class="val">n = <span id="nv">7</span></div>

      <div class="ctl">
        <label>minimum distance <em>d</em></label>
        <input type="range" id="d" min="1" max="24" value="3">
        <div class="val">d = <span id="dv">3</span></div>
      </div>
    </div>
    <div class="chips">
      <span class="chip" data-n="7"  data-d="3">the [7,4,3] Hamming code</span>
      <span class="chip" data-n="8"  data-d="4">its extension: A(8,4)</span>
      <span class="chip" data-n="15" data-d="3">the [15,11,3] Hamming code</span>
      <span class="chip" data-n="4"  data-d="3">no perfect code at length 4</span>
      <span class="chip" data-n="3"  data-d="2">the parity code</span>
      <span class="chip" data-n="12" data-d="8">the Plotkin regime</span>
    </div>

    <div class="bars" id="bars"></div>
    <div class="verdict" id="verdict"></div>

    <details>
      <summary>The four arguments, in one paragraph each</summary>
      <p><strong>Sphere packing.</strong> With minimum distance <code>2t+1</code> the balls of
      radius <code>t</code> around codewords cannot overlap — an overlap would put two codewords
      within <code>2t</code> of each other. Disjoint sets inside a universe of <code>2<sup>n</sup></code>
      words give <code>|C| · V(n,t) ≤ 2<sup>n</sup></code>, where
      <code>V(n,r) = Σ<sub>i≤r</sub> C(n,i)</code> is the ball volume.</p>
      <p><strong>Singleton.</strong> Keep only the first <code>n+1−d</code> coordinates. Two
      codewords agreeing there would differ only in the last <code>d−1</code> places, so
      truncation is injective and <code>|C| ≤ 2<sup>n+1−d</sup></code>.</p>
      <p><strong>Plotkin.</strong> Count the total pairwise distance twice. Every pair contributes
      at least <code>d</code>; and coordinate by coordinate, if <code>k</code> codewords carry a one
      there, the disagreeing ordered pairs number <code>2k(M−k) ≤ M²/2</code>. Squeezing gives
      <code>|C|(2d−n) ≤ 2d</code> whenever <code>n < 2d</code> — the only bound that survives
      when the distance is large relative to the length.</p>
      <p><strong>Gilbert–Varshamov (from below).</strong> Greedily add any word at distance
      <code>≥ d</code> from everything chosen so far. The result is maximal, so every word is within
      <code>d−1</code> of the code: the radius-<code>(d−1)</code> balls cover, giving
      <code>|C| · V(n,d−1) ≥ 2<sup>n</sup></code>.</p>
    </details>
  </div>

  <h2>The corridor, across all distances at this length</h2>
  <div class="panel">
    <canvas id="chart" width="1400" height="600"></canvas>
    <p class="sub" style="margin:10px 0 0">
      Logarithmic vertical axis. The shaded band between the best upper bound and the
      Gilbert–Varshamov lower bound is where <em>A</em>(<em>n</em>,<em>d</em>) must live; the
      band closes to a point exactly where the theory pins the value down.
    </p>

  <h2>Where the value is known exactly</h2>
  <div class="panel">
    <table id="exact"></table>
    <details>
      <summary>Why odd distances are the primitive ones</summary>
      <p>
        Append a parity bit to every codeword of a code with <em>odd</em> minimum distance
        <code>d</code>. All distances in the extended code become even — parity is the mod-2
        shadow of Hamming distance — and an even number that is at least the odd number
        <code>d</code> is at least <code>d+1</code>. So the extension has length <code>n+1</code>,
        distance <code>d+1</code>, and exactly as many codewords.
      </p>
      <p>
        Conversely, deleting the last coordinate of a code with distance <code>d+1 ≥ 2</code> is
        injective and costs at most one unit of distance. The two maps are mutually inverse on
        optimal codes, so <code>A(n,d) = A(n+1,d+1)</code> for every odd <code>d</code>. That is why
        code tables list only odd distances — and why "correct one error, detect two" costs exactly
        one extra bit and no codewords.
      </p>
      <p>
        The oddness matters: <code>A(3,2) = 4</code> but <code>A(4,3) ≤ 3</code>, so the identity is
        false at even <code>d</code>. Puncturing always works; extension is the fussy half.
      </p>
    </details>
  </div>
